props.title: Slaughterhouse-Five
props.initialSlug: Soldier unstuck in time relives war and alien abduction

sections.content: George Roy Hill's adaptation of Kurt Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse-Five (1972) stands as one of the most ambitious attempts to translate literary nonlinear storytelling to film. Like 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and The Bed-Sitting Room (1969), it embraces a deeply experimental structure while grappling with war's absurdity. Michael Sacks delivers a haunting performance as Billy Pilgrim, a man who becomes "unstuck in time," bouncing between his experiences as a POW during the Dresden bombing, his suburban American life, and his alleged adventures on the alien planet Tralfamadore.

sections.content: The film's groundbreaking editing techniques by Dede Allen influenced later nonlinear narratives like Memento (2000) and Arrival (2016). Rather than using conventional flashbacks, the cuts between time periods are abrupt and intentionally jarring, mirroring Billy's mental state and Vonnegut's prose style. The Dresden bombing sequences, filmed on location in Czechoslovakia, remain some of the most powerful anti-war imagery in cinema, later echoed in films like The Tin Drum (1979) and Come and See (1985).

Hill's direction balances the fantastical elements with stark realism, creating a dreamlike quality that influenced later magical realist war films like Empire of the Sun (1987) and Life is Beautiful (1997). The Tralfamadore sequences, with their retro-futuristic design, prefigure the metaphysical science fiction of Solaris (1972) and The Man Who Fell to Earth (1976). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Cinema

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond war movies and science fiction. Its technique of using temporal displacement to explore trauma can be seen in Jacob's Ladder (1990) and The Butterfly Effect (2004). The matter-of-fact treatment of extraordinary events established a template for magical realism in American cinema, paving the way for films like Being John Malkovich (1999) and Synecdoche, New York (2008).
